In this article TSLA Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT watch now VIDEO 2:48 02:48 Tesla reports 486,532 vehicle deliveries for third quarter, topping expectations Squawk on the Street Tesla just reported vehicle deliveries and production for the third quarter. Shares of Elon Musk' s EV maker climbed about 2% following the news. Here are the key numbers: Total Q3 vehicle deliveries: 486,532 Total Q3 vehicle production: 464,391 Deliveries fell about 2% from 497,099 a year earlier, but climbed from the second quarter, when Tesla recorded 480,126 deliveries. Analysts were expecting around 461,100 deliveries, according to StreetAccount's consensus. Tesla's company-compiled consensus , published Tuesday, was for 461,974 deliveries. Tesla doesn't break out exact delivery numbers by individual model or region, but the company said its entry-level Model 3 sedan and most popular Model Y SUVs accounted for a vast majority, or 98% , of its deliveries. Deliveries are the closest approximation of sales reported by Tesla but are not precisely defined in its shareholder communications. Musk's automaker is under pressure due to surging competition from Chinese electric vehicle makers, such BYD and Xiaomi, which sell more affordable and innovative EVs. Tesla is trying to recover from consecutive annual declines in vehicle sales that were partly caused by a consumer backlash against Musk, the world's wealthiest person, and by the loss of a U.S. federal tax credit. The Inflation Reduction Act, signed in 2022 by President Joe Biden, had made the EV tax break available through 2032. President Donald Trump's spending bill curtailed it ahead of schedule, ending the tax break after Sept. 30, 2025. Except Apple Tesla's stock is down 21% this year as of Tuesday's close, underperforming all of its megacap tech peers. Morgan Stanley analysts wrote in a note published Wednesday that Tesla's third-quarter deliveries would be a "tough comparison" to a year ago and the prior period. Last year's third period was Tesla's "record delivery quarter," they wrote, and in the second quarter, deliveries "exceeded production by roughly 28K vehicles." Tesla also said Friday that it deployed 13.7 GWh of energy storage products, including its Megapack and Megablock systems, during the quarter. A year ago Tesla deployed 12.5 GWh of such products, and last quarter that figure was 13.5 GWh. Megapacks are used for business and utility-scale developments, and Tesla's newer Megablocks are a combination of four Megapacks around one transformer. The systems use lithium-ion or other battery cells to help data centers and utilities avoid blackouts, allowing for energy storage from sources like solar and wind. Musk's SpaceX is a large buyer of Tesla's backup batteries, and has also purchased millions of dollars worth of its Cybertruck pickups. While Tesla is experiencing declines in deliveries, EV demand is up across the globe this year, according to a 2026 Global EV Outlook by the International Energy Agency. The IEA pointed to the Iran conflict and soaring gas prices as catalysts that "reinforced the case for EVs as a way to address energy security and fuel cost concerns." In 2020, EVs and hybrid electric models represented under 5% of new car sales worldwide. That share reached one in four new cars sold in 2025, according to IEA. Tesla said it will report third-quarter earnings on Oct. 21 after the market close. headlines.summary: YouTube is targeting more live sports rights. But it's more likely to buy games in bulk if there's a clear consumer proposition underlying the rights.
headlines.article_text: YouTube sports strategy targets more live rights -- but not necessarily events Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points YouTube is scanning the live sports landscape with interest in buying more rights. One strategy of YouTube's is to air some games on its massive free service and put most games on its subscription Premium service. YouTube is still wrestling with the feasibility of becoming the hub of all local games for the NBA starting in 2027. Subscribe here to get access today . Photo illustration of the YouTube TV logo displayed on a smartphone, with the YouTube logo in the background. Nurphoto | Nurphoto | Getty Images YouTube is stalking the sports landscape for live rights. YouTube would like as many games as it can get its hands on – while also giving users as "clean" of an experience as possible, according to people familiar with the matter. YouTube has been coy with its sports strategy, acquiring the rights to one NFL game last year for its free, ad-supported platform and buying "NFL Sunday Ticket" rights until the end of the 2029-30 season. Beyond those two moves, YouTube has largely been quiet. Still, YouTube is an interested buyer in live sports for almost all of the major U.S. sports leagues if it can get bespoke rights that present an easy consumer message, such as all local games or all games in a tournament, said the people, who asked not to be named because the company's plans are private. YouTube's strategy is distinct from Netflix's — an interesting contrast between the two largest streaming services in the world by users. While Netflix wants individual games or tournaments that it can turn into mini-events, YouTube is more likely to buy games in bulk if there's a clear consumer proposition underlying the rights. In other words, YouTube isn't interested in a swath of games if there's no obvious connection to them. Sports Business Journal reported earlier this year that YouTube is in advanced talks to be the NBA's new regional sports network solution, buying the rights for 20 to 25 teams for a price tag of potentially more than $1 billion. YouTube is interested in the FIFA Men's World Cup rights, as CNBC first reported in July. YouTube is still wrestling with the feasibility of this idea if it can't get all of the teams, said the people. YouTube ideally wants both in-market and out-of-market games, the people said. It's also unclear if the NBA is comfortable selling complete rights to one platform. A big part of YouTube's sports objective relates to building up its premium service. A few weeks ago, YouTube Premium struck a deal to ingest Peacock content within the service for no extra cost. YouTube Premium, which eliminates YouTube ads and costs $15.99 per month, doesn't necessarily want to strike a bunch of other similar deals and turn the service into an aggregator of other companies' streaming services. But what may interest YouTube executives is buying a chunk of live sports and putting it behind the paywall. In other words, making people pay for YouTube Premium to get access to the games. YouTube could then use "free" YouTube as its front-of-the-paywall marketing tool to get people to pay the monthly subscription fee for YouTube Premium. For example, it could put a small number of games on ad-supported YouTube to effectively advertise for signing up for the full package in Premium. It also can use its millions of sports-related content creator videos to push live games on Premium. YouTube hired Justin Connolly away from Disney last year to be its global head of media and sports. Connolly was one of Disney's highest paid executives, having spent 25 years at the company and rising through the ranks to become the company's president of platform distribution, including ESPN and Disney+. Sunday Ticket's fate NFL Commissioner Roger Goodell told CNBC last month the league could redo its existing packaging of games to better fit the modern media landscape. One way of doing this is to deconstruct "Sunday Ticket," which would give the league many more games to sell in other packages. YouTube executives are already considering this as a possibility, said the people. YouTube currently spends $2 billion per year on "Sunday Ticket" and could use that money and more to buy a new, premium package of games if the league moved in that direction. Wolfe Research analysts wrote a note to clients Friday predicting the NFL "will tier its rights in order to maximize the value of premium tiers while setting lower cost tiers to firms with more limited buying power." Josh Boland | Chicago Tribune | Tribune News Service | Getty Images Rivian Automotive on Friday reconfirmed its 2026 vehicle delivery guidance after reporting a year-over-year increase of 46% during the third quarter, topping Wall Street's expectations. The electric vehicle company reported delivery of 19,248 units from July through September, up from 13,201 a year earlier. Wall Street was expecting 18,000 units, according to average estimates compiled by FactSet. Rivian's 2026 guidance for vehicle deliveries, which it raised earlier this year, is between 65,000 and 70,000 vehicles. To achieve that target, the company would need to increase deliveries from the third to fourth quarters by at least 20.5%, to 23,193 vehicles.
